Angle[Self:imm]

The super type of Radian and Degree, used to enforce common behaviour Angles that normalize to the same value are considered equal, 360.0.degree .assertEq(0.0.degree) (Math.tau / -4.0).getRad.deg .assertEq((+3.0 / +4.0 * Math.tau).getRad.deg)

Byte

Byte: 8-bit unsigned [0,255]. Ordering is UNSIGNED.

Extends: Sealed, DataType[Byte,Byte], SumNumber[Byte], OrderHash[Byte], Order[Byte], Pipe[Byte], ToImm[Byte], ToInfo, ToStr, WidenTo[Byte]

Methods

▸read !=(read Byte):Bool

From: DataType[Byte,Byte]!=, OrderHash[Byte]!=, Order[Byte]!=.

▸**(Byte):Byte

this ** x returns the checked power of this raised to x. Throws if the result would exceed 255.

▸runnable example 
  .check{2.getByte ** (6.getByte) .assertEq(64.getByte)}
  .checkDetErr({_ -> True}, {2.getByte ** (8.getByte)})
▸*(Byte):Byte

this * x returns the checked product of this and x. Throws if the result would exceed 255.

▸runnable example 
  .check{10.getByte * (5.getByte) .assertEq(50.getByte)}
  .checkDetErr({_ -> True}, {100.getByte * (3.getByte)})
▸+(Byte):Byte

this + x returns the checked sum of this and x. Throws if the result would exceed 255.

▸runnable example 
  .check{(2.getByte + (3.getByte)) .assertEq(5.getByte)}
  .checkDetErr({_ -> True}, {(255.getByte) + (1.getByte)})
▸-(Byte):Byte

this - x returns the checked difference of this and x. Throws if the result would go below 0.

▸runnable example 
  .check{5.getByte - (3.getByte) .assertEq(2.getByte)}
  .checkDetErr({_ -> True}, {0.getByte - (1.getByte)})
▸.aluAddWrap(Byte):Byte

this.aluAddWrap(x) returns this + x mod 256 (u8 wraparound add).

▸runnable example 
  .check{250.getByte .aluAddWrap(10.getByte) .assertEq(4.getByte)}
▸.aluAnd(Byte):Byte

this.aluAnd(x) returns the bitwise AND of this and x.

▸runnable example 
  .check{5.getByte .aluAnd(3.getByte) .assertEq(1.getByte)}
▸.aluDiv(Byte):Byte

CapTry

This try-catch will catch non-deterministic errors.

Extends: ToIso[CapTry], WidenTo[CapTry]

Methods

▸mut #[R:*](read F[R]):mut Action[R]

This method upholds strong exception safety, so you can observe changes to the program state from any exception-causing code.

▸mut #[T:**,R:*](iso T,read F[iso T,R]):mut Action[R]

This method is designed to take an iso object capability to do effects while handling the non deterministic exception. However any violations of strong exception safety can only be observed with an object capability because the iso reference is not linked to the outer world, so it is conceptually data that could have equivalently been recreated internally.

DataTypeBy[E:imm,K:imm,K0:imm]

DataTypeBy is the "by key" conversion, analogous to OrderHashBy. It returns a closed DataType[K,K0] for each source value t: T. Examples: - If Key implements DataType[Key,Key0], then {::.key} : DataTypeBy[Foo,Key,Key0]. - {::} is the identity-by when T itself implements DataType[T,T0] (see DataTypeBy[T,T0] below).

ESet[E:imm]

A mutable set, allows for in place updates. In general this collection is built up with .add and similar methods and then consumed into a list. **NOTE:** Unlike Set this collection does not maintain a sorted order for performance.

Extends: Pipe[ESet[E]]

Methods

▸mut .add(E):mut ESet[E]

this.add(e) adds e to this and returns this to allow method chaining. Note this operation mutates this.

▸runnable example 
  .check{ESets#{::}.add(1).add(2).add(3).set.str .assertEq "{1, 2, 3}"}
▸mut .addAll(ESet[E]):mut ESet[E]

this.addAll eset adds all of the elements of eset to this without draining eset. Note this operation mutates this.

▸runnable example 
  .let eset={ESets#[Nat, Nat]{::}.add(1).add(2)}
  .check{eset.addAll(Flows#(2,3,4).eset({::}, {::})).size == 4}
▸mut .clear:mut ESet[E]

this.clear removes all the elements from this and returns this to allow method chaining. Note this operation mutates this.

▸runnable example 
  .let eset={ESets#[Nat, Nat]{::}.add(1).add(2)}
  .check{eset.size .assertEq 2}
  .check{eset.clear.isEmpty .assertTrue}
  .check{eset.isEmpty .assertTrue}
▸mut .close:mut ESet[E]

From: Pipe[ESet[E]].close.

▸read .close:read ESet[E]

From: Pipe[ESet[E]].close.

▸read .contains(E):Bool

this.contains(e) returns True if e is present in this.

▸runnable example 
  .let eset={ESets#[Nat,Nat]{::}.add(1).add(2)}
  .check{eset.contains(1) .assertTrue}
  .check{eset.contains(3) .assertFalse}
▸read .containsAll(ESet[E]):Bool

this.contains(e) returns True if e is present in this.

▸runnable example 
  .let eset={ESets#[Nat,Nat]{::}.add(1).add(2)}
  .let inner={ESets#{::} .add 1}
  .check{eset.containsAll(inner) .assertTrue}
  .check{eset.contains(inner.add(3)) .assertFalse}
▸mut .distinctBy[K:imm](OrderHashBy[imm E,K]):mut ESet[E]

this.distinctBy(by) replaces the orderHash of this with by and returns this. This may cause elements in this to be removed if they are equal under by. Note this operation mutates this.

▸runnable example 
  .check{ESets#[Int, Int]{::}
    .add(+1).add(-2).add(+3)
    .distinctBy({::.imm.sign}).set.str{::} .assertEq "{+1, -2}"}
▸mut .flow:mut Flow[E]

this.flow returns a potentially parallel flow over the elements of this. Note this operation drains this, so any future accesses to this will point to an empty ESet.

▸runnable example 
  .let eset={ESets#[Int, Int]{::}.add(+1).add(-2).add(+3)}
  .check{eset.flow.list.str{::} .assertEq "[+1, -2, +3]"}
  .check{eset.isEmpty .assertTrue}
▸mut .get(E):E

this.get(e) returns the element in this equal to e under this's orderHash throws if no such element exists.

▸runnable example 
  .check{Sets#({::.imm.abs}, +1, -2).get(-1) .assertEq +1}
  .checkDetErr({_ -> True}, {Sets#({::}, 1, 2).get(3)})
▸mut .getOrInsert(E):E

this.getOrInsert(e) returns the element in this equal to e under this's orderHash, inserting it first if it doesn't exist;

▸runnable example 
  .let eset={Flows(+1, -2).eset({::}, {::.imm.abs})}
  .check{eset.getOrInsert(-1) .assertEq +1}
  .check{eset.getOrInsert(+3) .assertEq +3}
  .check{eset.size .assertEq 3}
▸mut .getTake(E):E

this.getTake(e) removes and returns e, throws if it doesn't exist.

▸runnable example 
  .let eset={Flows(+1, -2).eset({::}, {::.imm.abs})}
  .check{eset.take(-1)! .assertEq +1}
  .check{eset.take(-1).isEmpty .assertTrue}
  .check{eset.size .assertEq 1}
▸read .isEmpty:Bool

this.isEmpty returns True if this has no elements. Equivalent to: this.size == 0

▸runnable example 
  .let s={ESets#[Nat, Nat]{::}}
  .check{s.isEmpty .assertTrue}
  .check{s.add(1).isEmpty .assertFalse}
▸read .notEmpty:Bool

this.notEmpty returns True if this has any elements. Equivalent to: this.isEmpty.not

▸runnable example 
  .let s={ESets#[Nat, Nat] {::}}
  .check{s.notEmpty .assertFalse}
  .check{s.add(1).notEmpty .assertTrue}
▸mut .opt(E):mut Opt[E]

this.opt(e) returns .some of the element in this equal to e under this's orderHash returns .empty if no such element exists.

▸runnable example 
  .check{Sets#({::.imm.abs}, +1, -2).opt(-1)! .assertEq +1}
  .check{Sets#({::}, 1, 2).opt(3).isEmpty .assertTrue}
▸read .orderHash:OrderHashBy[E]

The orderHash used to determine equality, hashing and potentially ordering of elements in this set.

▸mut .remove(E):ESet[E]

this.remove e removes e from this set if it is present, and returns this.

▸runnable example 
  .check{ESets#{::} .add 2 .add 3 .remove 2 .remove 3 .isEmpty .assertTrue}
  .check{ESets#{::} .add 1 .remove 2 .contains 1 .assertTrue}
▸mut .removeAll(ESet[E]):mut ESet[E]

this.removeAll eset removes all of the elements of eset from this without draining eset. Note this operation mutates this.

▸runnable example 
  .let eset={ESets#[Nat, Nat]{::}.add(1).add(2)}
  .check{eset.removeAll(Flows#(2,3,4).eset({::}, {::})).size == 1}
▸mut .removeIf(mut MF[E,Bool]):mut ESet[E]

this.removeIf(f) removes all elements for which f returns True, returning this.

▸mut .retainIf(mut MF[E,Bool]):mut ESet[E]

this.retainIf(f) removes all elements for which f returns False, returning this. Equivalent to: this.removeIf{e -> f#e .not}

this.seqFlow returns a sequential flow over the elements of this. Note this operation drains this, so any future accesses to this will point to an empty ESet.

▸runnable example 
  .let eset={ESets#[Int, Int]{::}.add(+1).add(-2).add(+3)}
  .check{eset.seqFlow.list.str{::} .assertEq "[+1, -2, +3]"}
  .check{eset.isEmpty .assertTrue}
▸mut .set:Set[E]

this.set returns a Set of all the elements of this. Note this operation drains this, so any future accesses to this will point to an empty ESet.

▸runnable example 
  .let eset={ESets#[Int, Int]{::}.add(+1).add(-2).add(+3)}
  .check{eset.set.str .assertEq "{+1, -2, +3}"}
  .check{eset.isEmpty .assertTrue}
▸read .size:Nat

this.size returns the number of elements in this.

▸runnable example 
  .check{ESets#[Nat, Nat]({::}).add(1).add(2).add(3).size .assertEq 3}
  .check{ESets#[Nat, Nat]({::}).size .assertEq 0}
▸mut .take(E):Opt[E]

this.take(e) removes and returns e if it exists, otherwise returns .empty

▸runnable example 
  .let eset={Flows(+1, -2).eset({::}, {::.imm.abs})}
  .check{eset.take(-1)! .assertEq +1}
  .check{eset.take(-1).isEmpty .assertTrue}
  .check{eset.size .assertEq 1}

Error

Exception classes (observability): - deterministic: The same operation called with observationally identical input will either always throw or never throw. Catchable anywhere via Try#. - nonDeterministic: the throw may or may not happen in the same abstract situation (OOM, stack overflow, asserts, etc). Catching/observing requires mut CapTry obtained from mut System.

Asserts are nonDeterministic because another standard library may legally replace them with no-ops.

Float

Float: 64 bits IEEE values. Note: ==/order instead follow the usual rules: - NaN == NaN (all different NaNs equal); NaN is greater than everything else including +Inf - -0.0 == +0.0 Method hash must respect this ordering

Extends: Sealed, DataType[Float,Float], SumNumber[Float], _AssertApprox[Float], DataType[Float,Float], OrderHash[Float], Order[Float], Pipe[Float], ToImm[Float], ToInfo, ToStr, WidenTo[Float]

▸**(Float):Float

this ** x returns the this raised to the power x. Never throws; NaN propagates Note: This differs from this.ieeePow as it relaxes the assumption that infinities are effectively large even integers, and removes special rules precedence, in general if a**x = b for all x, and y**c = d for all y, then y**x == (Math.nan) if c!=d: - x**(Math.inf) for x < 0.0, +/-0.0 ** +/-0.0, Math.inf ** 0.0 all return Math.nan`

▸runnable example 
  .check{2.0 ** 3.0 .assertEq 8.0}
  .check{Math.nan ** 0.0 .isNaN .assertTrue} // not true of ieee
  .check{0.0 ** -0.0 .isNaN .assertTrue}  // not true of ieee
▸*(Float):Float

this * x returns the IEEE 754 product of this and x. Never throws; NaN propagates.

▸runnable example 
  .check{2.0 * 3.0 .assertEq 6.0}
  .check{0.0 * (Math.inf) .isNaN .assertTrue}
▸+(Float):Float

this + x returns the IEEE 754 sum of this and x. Never throws; NaN propagates.

▸runnable example 
  .check{2.0 + 3.0 .assertEq 5.0}
  .check{Math.inf + 1.0 .assertEq(Math.inf)}
  .check{Math.nan + 1.0 .isNaN .assertTrue}
▸-(Float):Float

this - x returns the IEEE 754 difference of this and x. Never throws; NaN propagates.

▸runnable example 
  .check{5.0 - 3.0 .assertEq 2.0}
  .check{Math.inf - (Math.inf) .isNaN .assertTrue}

this.abs returns .some of this if this >= 0, .some of -this if this < 0, .empty if this is NaN.

▸runnable example

  .check{-4.75 .abs .assertEq({::}, Opts# 4.75)}
  .check{Math.nan .abs .assertEmpty}
▸.absOrNaN:Float

this.absOrNaN returns the IEEE absolute value of this: this if this >= 0, -this if this < 0, and Math.nan if this is NaN (payload preserved semantics not guaranteed).

  .check{-4.75 .absOrNaN .assertEq 4.75}

▸.ieeeEq(Float):Bool

this.ieeeEq(x) return true if this equals x according to the IEEE standard. Note: this differs from Fearless == as Math.nan.ieeeEq(Math.nan) is false

▸runnable example 
  .check{Math.nan.ieeeEq(Math.nan).assertFalse}
  .check{+0.0 .ieeeEq -0.0  .assertTrue}
▸.ieeePow(Float):Float

this.ieeePow(x) returns the IEEE 754-2008 pow(this, x), following the full IEEE special-value rules unlike ** - see its docs for how the two differ. Rules apply top down - x.ieeePow(+/-0.0) is +1.0 for any x including Math.nan, +/-0.0, ; - (+/-0.0).ieeePow(y) is: - +/-Math.inf if y is negative odd integer, - Math.inf if y is Math.negInf, - +0.0 if y is Math.inf - Math.inf is considered a large positive integer, - Math.inf for finite y < 0 that is not an odd integer, - +/-0.0 for finite y > 0 an odd integer - +0.0 for finite y > 0 that is not an odd integer; - -1.0.ieeePow(+/-Math.inf) is 1.0; - 1.0.ieeePow(y) is 1.0 for any y - even Math.nan; - x.ieeePow(y) is Math.nan for finite x < 0 and finite non-integer y.

▸.ieeeRemainder(Float):Float

this.ieeeRemainder(d) returns the IEEE remainder r = this - n*d, where n is the integer nearest this/d (ties-to-even).

▸runnable example 
  .check{5.0 .ieeeRemainder 3.0 .assertEq -1.0}
▸.ieeeSameBits(Float):Bool

this.ieeeSameBits(x) compares raw bit patterns: distinguishes NaN payloads and signed zero (unlike ieeeEq and the type's own ==).

▸runnable example 
  .check{(0.0 .ieeeSameBits(-0.0)) .assertFalse}
  .check{(1.0 .ieeeSameBits 1.0) .assertTrue}
▸.ieeeStr:Str

this.ieeeStr returns an IEEE 754 round-trip decimal string for this (includes NaN/Inf). NaN payloads are not distinguished (all NaNs render identically); use ieeeSameBits for that.

▸runnable example 
  .check{1.5 .ieeeStr .assertEq "1.5"}

  .check{(2.0 .inRange(1.0=~~=4.0)) .assertTrue}
  .check{(5.0 .inRange(1.0=~~=4.0)) .assertFalse}

▸.int:Opt[Int]

this.int returns .some of this as an Int if this is an integer in [minInt, maxInt], .empty otherwise (non-integral, out of range, NaN, or infinite).

▸runnable example 
  .check{3.0 .int .assertEq({::}, Opts# +3)}
  .check{3.5 .int .assertEmpty}
  .check{Math.nan .int .assertEmpty}
▸.isFinite:Bool

this.isFinite returns True if this is not Math.nan, Math.inf, or Math.negInf. Note: this is not equivalent to this.isInfinite.not, since both are False for Math.nan.

▸runnable example 
  .check{1.0 .isFinite .assertTrue}
  .check{0.0 .isFinite .assertTrue}
  .check{Math.inf .isFinite .assertFalse}
  .check{Math.nan .isFinite .assertFalse}
▸.isInfinite:Bool

this.isInfinite returns True iff this is Math.inf or Math.negInf.

  .check{Math.inf .isInfinite .assertTrue}
  .check{Math.negInf .isInfinite .assertTrue}
  .check{1.0 .isInfinite .assertFalse}

▸.match[R:*](mut FloatMatch[R]):R

this.match(m) dispatches on the special variants of float weirdness: +0.0, -0.0, +Inf, -Inf, NaN, or a regular finite/non-special value.

▸runnable example 
  .check{(0.0 .match({.posZero -> "pz"; .negZero -> "nz"; .posInf -> "pi"; .negInf -> "ni"; .nan -> "n"; .regular x -> "r"})) .assertEq "pz"}
  .check{(3.5 .match({.posZero -> "pz"; .negZero -> "nz"; .posInf -> "pi"; .negInf -> "ni"; .nan -> "n"; .regular x -> "r"})) .assertEq "r"}
  .check{((Math.nan) .match({.posZero -> "pz"; .negZero -> "nz"; .posInf -> "pi"; .negInf -> "ni"; .nan -> "n"; .regular x -> "r"})) .assertEq "n"}

InMemoryLog[T:imm]

Logs values in memory.

Use by defining a capture-free singleton log: ``` PointLog: InMemoryLog[Point]{"PointLog"} ...//usage PointLog.log(myPoint) ..//later, reading the log and confirming is what we expect PointLog.reader(sys).consume.assertEq({::},Lists#(myPoint)) ```

In memory logs are particularly useful for unit testing of immutable computation via mock objects.

The name is only diagnostic, to be used for debugging, test reports, and failure messages. Two different logs with the same name do not interfere with each other.

The log is kept in runtime memory. Calling .log appends a value to the current in-memory contents of this log.

Calling .reader creates a reader for this log through System. The reader can inspect or consume the values currently stored for this log.

Concrete log types must be non generic. Creating a reader throw with nondeterministic error if the concrete log type is generic.

Extends: CaptureFree

Methods

▸.log(T):Void

Submits s to an in memory log that requires a capability to be read.

Int

Int: signed 64-bit. Note: / is not provided; use div/rem (divisor is Nat).

Extends: Sealed, DataType[Int,Int], SumNumber[Int], OrderHash[Int], Order[Int], Pipe[Int], ToImm[Int], ToInfo, ToStr, WidenTo[Int]

Methods

▸read !=(read Int):Bool

From: DataType[Int,Int]!=, OrderHash[Int]!=, Order[Int]!=.

▸**(Nat):Int

this ** x returns the checked power of this raised to x. Note: x is Nat (not Int), as negative exponents would produce fractional results. Throws on overflow/underflow.

▸runnable example 
  .check{(+2 ** 6) .assertEq +64}
  .checkDetErr({_ -> True}, {(Math.maxInt) ** 2})
▸*(Int):Int

this * x returns the checked product of this and x. Throws on overflow/underflow.

▸runnable example

Log

Log strings in a text file.

The log is written to .out/logs/_base/log.log. Each call appends the string representation of s as one timestamped line. The timestamp is in UTC and is added by the runtime.

The log is circular across runs: - when logging starts, an existing non-empty live log is moved to a stamped archive file; - when the program shuts down, the current non-empty live log is also moved to a stamped archive file; - empty live logs are deleted; - only a bounded number of archived logs is kept. (currently 10, this may change with future versions)

If a previous live log is found when logging starts, the archived copy is marked as interrupted. This usually means the previous process did not complete normal shutdown.

Logging failures are reported to the runtime error log when possible. Only a bounded number of error logs is kept. (currently 100, this may change with future versions)

Math

Question: How many methods should be added here? Stuff like .abs and .sqrt are defined on the numeric types themselves, so they are not included here, should they be? What about .sin, .cos, .tan, .log, .exp, etc? Should they be included here? What about other constants like Pi and E? When do they get too obscure to be worth including here?

▸**(Nat):Nat

this ** x returns the checked power of this raised to x. Throws on overflow.

▸runnable example 
  .check{(2 ** 6) .assertEq 64}
  .checkDetErr({_ -> True}, {(Math.maxNat) ** 2})
▸*(Nat):Nat

this * x returns the checked product of this and x. Throws on overflow.

▸runnable example 
  .check{(6 * 7) .assertEq 42}
  .checkDetErr({_ -> True}, {(Math.maxNat) * 2})
▸+(Nat):Nat

this + x returns the checked sum of this and x. Throws on overflow past Math.maxNat.

▸runnable example 
  .check{(2 + 3) .assertEq 5}
  .checkDetErr({_ -> True}, {(Math.maxNat - 1) + 2})
▸-(Nat):Nat

this - x returns the checked difference of this and x. Throws on underflow below 0.

▸runnable example 
  .check{(5 - 3) .assertEq 2}
  .checkDetErr({_ -> True}, {0 - 1})
▸.aluAddWrap(Nat):Nat

this.aluAddWrap(x) returns this + x mod 2^64 (u64 wraparound add)

▸runnable example 
  .check{(Math.maxNat) .aluAddWrap 1 .assertEq 0}
▸.aluAnd(Nat):Nat

this.aluAnd(x) returns the bitwise AND of this and x (u64)

▸runnable example 
  .check{5 .aluAnd 3 .assertEq 1}
▸.aluByte:Byte

this.aluByte returns the low 8 bits of this, wrapped (not clamped).

▸runnable example 
  .check{257 .aluByte .assertEq(1.getByte)}
▸.aluDiv(Nat):Nat

this.aluDiv(x) returns this divided by x, truncated toward 0 (u64 semantics). Throws iff x == 0.

▸runnable example 
  .check{7 .aluDiv 2 .assertEq 3}
  .checkDetErr({_ -> True}, {7 .aluDiv 0})
▸.aluInt:Int

this.aluInt reinterprets the raw u64 bits of this as a signed i64 Int (bit-cast, not a value conversion).

▸runnable example 
  .check{(Math.maxNat) .aluInt .assertEq -1}
▸.aluMulWrap(Nat):Nat

this.aluMulWrap(x) returns this * x mod 2^64 (u64 wraparound mul)

▸runnable example 
  .check{(Math.maxNat) .aluMulWrap 2 .assertEq(Math.maxNat - 1)}
▸.aluOr(Nat):Nat

this.aluOr(x) returns the bitwise OR of this and x (u64)

▸runnable example 
  .check{5 .aluOr 2 .assertEq 7}
▸.aluRem(Nat):Nat

this.aluRem(x) returns the remainder paired with this.aluDiv(x). Throws iff x == 0.

▸runnable example 
  .check{7 .aluRem 2 .assertEq 1}
  .checkDetErr({_ -> True}, {7 .aluRem 0})
▸.aluShiftLeft(Nat):Nat

▸runnable example 
  .check{1 .aluShiftLeft 3 .assertEq 8}
▸.aluShiftRight(Nat):Nat

this.aluShiftRight(bits) returns this logically shifted right by bits, with the effective shift taken modulo 64 (bits & 63)

▸runnable example 
  .check{8 .aluShiftRight 3 .assertEq 1}
▸.aluSubWrap(Nat):Nat

▸.assertInRange(Range[Nat]):Void

this.assertInRange(range) asserts this.inRange(range), using a default empty message. Note: This method calls .str method on the non-sealed range, meaning you should be careful to call this on a range you do not control, as doing so may invoke arbitrary code.

▸runnable example 
  .check{2 .assertInRange(1=~~=4)}
  .checkNonDetErr({_ -> True}, {5 .assertInRange(1=~~=4)})
▸.assertInRange(Range[Nat],read LazyInfo):Void

this.assertInRange(range, msg) asserts this.inRange(range) with custom error message. Note: This method calls .str method on the non-sealed range, meaning you should be careful to call this on a range you do not control, as doing so may invoke arbitrary code.

▸runnable example 
  .check{2 .assertInRange(1=~~=4, {`custom context`})}

▸**(Int):Num

this ** x raises this to the power x. x is an Int (not Num), since fractional exponents could produce results that aren't expressible as an exact rational.

  .check{(2/4 ** +3) .assertEq(8 / 64)}
  .check{(2/1 ** -1) .assertEq(1 / 2)}

Operation[S:**,R:**]

An operation is a pipeable function that takes an S -> R, and can be piped into other operations. This can be useful to improve code readability by avoiding nested function calls. This allows for function piping from functional languages, is similar to extension methods from OOP languages Examples:

▸runnable example 
  .check{Math.ln(Math.asin(Math.clamp({::}, -1.0, +1.0, 12.0))#)
    .assertEq(12.0 |> {Math.clamp({::}, -1.0, +1.0, ::)} |> {Math.asin :: #} |> Math.ln)}

Range[N:imm]

A datatype to represent a discrete range of comparable values. Note: For the discrete numeric types, the core logic of these methods is implemented in those types, so it is safe when implementing a new Range of those types to call those methods, without it going in loop. Warning: Because of this, if you define your own discrete type that overrides .contains or .clamp the symmetry of these methods will be broken, That is MyRange.contains(n) may not be equivalent to n.inRange(n)

Extends: Container[N], Pipe[Range[N]], ToStr

Set[E:imm]

The implementation of a Set[E] the set keys must be imm to prevent breaking set invariants through mutating it's contents. This set is immutable so this + e will produce a new set with e included, and will not change this. This set maintains a sorted list of elements, such that the set ordering is predictable given the OrderHash.

Extends: Sealed, DataType[Set[E],Set[E],E,E], OrderHash[Set[E],E], Order[Set[E],E], Pipe[Set[E]], ToImm[E,E,Set[E]], ToInfo[E], ToStr[E], WidenTo[Set[E]]

Methods

▸&(Set[E]):Set[E]

this & other returns the intersection of this and other, using this's orderHash. Equivalent to: this.intersection(this.orderHash, other)

▸runnable example 
  .let s1={Sets#({::}, 1, 2)}
  .let s2={Sets#({::}, 2, 3)}
  .check{s1 & s2 .assertEq({::}, Sets#({::}, 2))}
▸++(Set[E]):Set[E]

this ++ other returns the union of this and other, using this's orderHash. Equivalent to this.union(this.orderHash, other), and this.union(other).

▸runnable example 
  .let s1={Sets#({::}, 1, 2)}
  .let s2={Sets#({::}, 2, 3)}
  .check{s1 ++ s2 .assertEq({::}, Sets#({::}, 1, 2, 3))}
▸+(E):Set[E]

this + e returns a new Set[E] containing all elements of this plus e. Returns this if this.contains e.

▸runnable example 
  .check{Sets#({::}, 1) + 2 .assertEq({::}, Sets#({::}, 1, 2))}
  .check{Sets#({::.imm.abs.getInt}, +1) + -1 .assertEq({::}, Sets#({::}, +1))}
▸--(Set[E]):Set[E]

this -- other returns a set containing the elements in this that are not in other, using this's orderHash. Equivalent to: this.difference(this.orderHash, other)

▸runnable example 
  .let s1={Sets#({::}, 1, 2, 3)}
  .let s2={Sets#({::}, 2)}
  .check{s1 -- s2 .assertEq({::}, Sets#({::}, 1, 3))}
▸-(E):Set[E]

this - e returns a new Set[E] containing all elements of this except e. Returns this if this did not contain e.

▸runnable example 
  .check{Sets#({::}, 2, 3) - 2 - 3 .isEmpty .assertTrue}
  .check{Sets#({::}, 1) - 2 .assertEq({::}, Sets#({::}, 1))}

From: DataType[Set[E],Set[E],E,E].close, OrderHash[Set[E],E].close.

▸.cmp[R:**](read Set[E],read Set[E],mut OrderMatch[R]):R

this.cmp(a, b, m) compares sets a and b using this's orderHash. Equivalent to this.cmp(this.orderHash, a, b, m). Note the ordering of the set elements is given by their orderHash, not the given by. if you want two sets ignoring their original order, you should use this.setCmp

▸runnable example 
  .let s1={Sets#({::}, +1, +2, +3)}
  .let s2={Sets#({::}, -2, -3, -1)}
  .check{Sets#[Int,Int]({::.imm.abs.getInt}).cmp(s1, s2, {.eq -> 0; .lt -> 1; .gt -> 2}) .assertEq 1}
▸read .cmp[_AAAK:imm,_AR:**](OrderBy[imm E,_AAAK],read Set[E],read Set[E],mut OrderMatch[_AR]):_AR

this.cmp(by, a, b, m) compares sets a and b using by. Returns m.eq if a and b contain the same elements under by. If unequal, returns m.gt if the first non-equal element of a is greater than the first non-equal element of b, or all elements are equal and a is larger. Note the ordering of the set elements is given by their orderHash, not the given by. Returns m.lt otherwise. if you want two sets ignoring their original order, you should use this.setCmp

▸runnable example 
  .let empty={Sets#[Nat,Nat]({::})}
  .check{empty.cmp({::}, Sets#({::}, 1, 2, 3), Sets#({::}, 2, 3, 1), {.eq -> 0; .lt -> 1; .gt -> 2}) .assertEq 0}
  .check{empty.cmp({::}, Sets#({::}, 3, 1, 2), Sets#({::}, 0, 1, 2, 3),  {.eq -> 0; .lt -> 1; .gt -> 2}) .assertEq 1}
  .check{empty.cmp({::}, Sets#({::}, 1, 2, 3), Sets#({::}, 1, 2), {.eq -> 0; .lt -> 1; .gt -> 2}) .assertEq 2}

From: DataType[Set[E],Set[E],E,E].cmp, OrderHash[Set[E],E].cmp, Order[Set[E],E].cmp.

▸.contains(E):Bool

this.contains(e) returns True if e is present in this.

▸runnable example 
  .check{Sets#({::}, 1).contains(1) .assertTrue}
  .check{Sets#({::}, 0).contains(1) .assertFalse}
▸.containsAll(Set[E]):Bool

this.containsAll(other) returns True if every element of other is present in this, using this's orderHash. Equivalent to: this.containsAll(this.orderHash, other)

▸runnable example 
  .let s1={Sets#({::}, 1, 2, 3)}
  .check{s1.containsAll(Sets#({::}, 1, 2)) .assertTrue}
  .check{s1.containsAll(Sets#({::}, 1, 2, 4)) .assertFalse}
▸.containsAll[K:imm](OrderHashBy[E,K],Set[E]):Bool

this.containsAll(by, other) returns True if every element of other is present in this, using by to determine equality.

▸runnable example 
  .check{Sets#({::}, +1, +2).containsAll({::.imm.abs}, Sets#({::}, -1, -2)) .assertTrue}
  .check{Sets#({::}, +1, +2).containsAll({::.imm.abs}, Sets#({::}, -1, -3)) .assertFalse}
▸read .dataType[_AK:imm](DataTypeBy[imm E,_AK,E]):read DataType[Set[E],Set[E]]

From: DataType[Set[E],Set[E],E,E].dataType.

▸.difference[K:imm](OrderHashBy[E,K],Set[E]):Set[E]

this.difference(by, other) returns a new set with all elements of other removed from this, using the given by to determine equality.

▸runnable example 
  .let s1={Sets#({::}, +1, +2, +3)}
  .let s2={Sets#({::}, +2)}
  .check{s1.difference({::}, s2) .assertEq({::}, Sets#({::}, +1, +3))}
  .check{s1.difference({::.imm.abs.getInt}, Sets#({::}, -2)) .assertEq({::}, Sets#({::}, +1, +3))}
▸.distinctBy[K:imm](OrderHashBy[E,K]):Set[E]

this.distinctBy(by) returns a new set with all the elements of this using by's orderHash. Note: - this new set may not contain all of the elements of this as elements that are considered equal under by will be deduplicated. - The complexity of this operation is O(nlog(n)) as it needs to sort the elements of this usingby.

▸runnable example 
  .let s={Sets#({::}, +1, -1, +2, -2)}
  .check{s.distinctBy({::.imm.abs}).str{::} .assertEq "{-1, -2}"}
▸.flow:mut Flow[E]

▸read .hash[_AAK:imm](OrderHashBy[imm E,_AAK]):Nat

this.hash(by) returns a hash of this set using by to hash each element. The hash is seeded with the size of this set, then each element's hash is folded in. Note: lists and sets use the same hash algorithm; two collections with the same elements in the same order will produce the same hash.

▸runnable example

    .assertEq(Sets#({::}, 3, 1, 2).hash{::})}

Str

Simple string type This string type is designed for robustness and ease of reasoning. It can only even contain the following whitelisted characters: 0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ+-*/=<>,.;:()[]{}`'"!?@#$%^&_|~\ Plus space and new line. There is no concept of escape as in some other languages, so \n is two characters. The methods ^ and | can be used to obtain a string including new lines or backticks (`).

Relations of parsers and printers. Methods .getInt/.getFloat/.getNum/.getByte below accept exactly the numeric type names accepted by the Fearless syntax, including the allowed _ as for the Fearless syntax. They *do not* evaluate expressions. Str.escape, Float.str and Float.ieeeStr instead output Fearless code when there is no literal represing the value.

Str.getInt: - rejected: 12.getInt +1_.getInt +_1.getInt - accepted: +12.getInt, +1_000.getInt +0__10.getInt +01__0.getInt +1__0.getInt +00.getInt -00.getInt -001.getInt +001.getInt - canonicalization: +00_12.getInt.str ==+12

Str.getNat: - rejected: +12.getNat -1.getNat 1_.getNat _1.getNat 4_294_967_296.getNat (range) - accepted: 0.getNat 00.getNat 0__10.getNat 4_294_967_295.getNat - canonicalization: 000_255.nat.str ==255 and 4_294_967_295.nat.str==4294967295

Str.getByte: - rejected: +12.getByte -1.getByte 1_.getByte _1.getByte 256.getByte - accepted: 0.getByte 00.getByte 0__10.getByte 255.getByte 000_255.getByte - canonicalization: 000_255.getByte.str==255

Str.getNum: - rejected: 12.getNum +12.getNum +1/.getNum +1./2.getNum +1/_2.getNum +1/0.getNum +1.0/0.0.getNum - accepted: +12/1.getNum -00_12/000_3.getNum +12.4/3.2.getNum +0/1.getNum -0/1.getNum - canonicalization: +12.4/3.2.getNum!.str==+31/8 +12/2.getNum!.str==+6/1

Str.getFloat (IEEE 754 binary 64): - rejected (syntax): 1.0.getFloat +1.getFloat +1..getFloat +.1.getFloat +1e0.getFloat - rejected (value): +NaN.getFloat +Infinity.getFloat -Infinity.getFloat +0.1.getFloat - Float value 0.1 (and many others) do not exist; so it is rejected. - accepted: +0.5.getFloat +1.25.getFloat +01__0.00__1.getFloat +1.0e-3.getFloat - canonicalization: -0.0.getFloat.str==+0.0

Str.ieeeFloat: - rejected: duck.ieeeFloat - accepted: NaN.ieeeFloat Infinity.ieeeFloat -Infinity.ieeeFloat -0.0.ieeeFloat +0.0.ieeeFloat 1e0.ieeeFloat - canonicalization: 1e0.ieeeFloat!.ieeeStr==1.0 and +0.0.ieeeFloat!.ieeeStr==0.0 (NaN payload not preserved) - roundtrip (value): f.ieeeStr.ieeeFloat! == f The roundtrip also preserves the sign of zero but not the NaN payload 0.1.ieeeFloat!.ieeeStr == 0.1 BUT there is no Float representing 0.1 .ieeeFloat + .ieeeStr implement shortest string that round-trips under round-to-nearest ties-to-even That is, 0.1.ieeeFloat!.ieeeStr lies to you twice, once when it creates the float, and a secon time when it choses to print a near value that has a compact representation instead of the actual content of the float Another example: 0.100000000000000005.ieeeFloat!.ieeeStr == 0.1 But, 0.100000000000000005 is closer to the actual representable Float value. That is, +0.1.ieeeFloat!.getNum!.inRange(+0.100000000000000005/1, +2/1) holds +0.1.ieeeFloat!.getNum!.inRange(+0.1/1, +0.100000000000000005/1) does not hold

Float.ieeeStr.ieeeFloat produces the same Float modulo NaN payload; but Str.ieeeFloat.ieeeStr may not produce the same string due to canonicalization+rounding)

ToImm[T0:imm]

DataType sits on top of OrderHash: Order > OrderHash > DataType It adds: - Info (for easy serialization/deserialization/exceptions) - deep imm conversion - widen/equality helpers (defined elsewhere)

Fixpoint story: - OrderHash[T] already provides the method .close: T allowing to see this as a T - DataType adds the opposite direction .close(t: T): DataType[...] allowing to this T as DataType[T] Basically, by implementing those two methods we close the type fixpoint making T and the DataType the same logical type.

ToStr

Ordering + hashing via "closed fixpoints". Intuition: - An Order[T] is a comparator that is also a *closed* value: .close: T. - Most concrete T implement Order[T] with .close->this. - OrderBy[T,K] is a projection: given t: T, build a closed Order[K] for its key. - OrderHash adds hashing and ToStr. This is all the Maps/Set may need.

UStr

Unicode string type This string type is designed to support the evil concept of Unicode strings. UStr is an intentionally minimal type representing a sequence of Nats in the ranges 0..55295 and 57344..1114111. Yes, there is a hole in the allowed values, as required by the Unicode standard for 'scalar values'.

Those numbers are conventionally written in hexadecimal (base 16) using digits 0..9 and letters A..F; total of 16 symbols representing numbers 0-15 with a single symbol each. For example, 0061 is the scalar value for a, and 1F600 is the scalar value for the grinning face emoji. Unicode documentation often writes those same numbers as U+0061 and U+1F600.

Crucially, there are no UStr literals. Use the method .u on Str to obtain Unicode strings. `foo`.u converts the foo Str into the equivalent UStr. The method .u on UStr reads one or more uppercase hexadecimal numbers separated by single spaces, and appends the corresponding scalar values. Only digits 0..9 and uppercase letters A..F are allowed. No extra whitespace is accepted. Malformed input throws. For example: `Hello`.u.u`FB03 0066 0066 0069`+(`World`.u) would create a string that may be visualized as "HelloffiffiWorld", but where the first ffi is represented as a single scalar value representing a ligature, while the second ffi is represented as three distinct scalar values. And myUString.u`FB03 0066 0066 0069`+(`Hello`.u) would append "ffiffiHello" to a pre-existing Unicode string. Since writing `Hello`.u.u`...` is clearly redundant, Str also supports .u with one argument, that first converts to unicode and then append the new sequence.

This type does support concatenation (+,|,^) as for Str, but this works by simply apppending scalar values one after the other in the sequence. This may not be desirable. Consider ligatures (where scalar values could/should/may be merged) and grapheme clusters, where simply sequencing scalar values may accidentally create new undesired grapheme clusters. More complex methods, like .startsWith(prefix) and .replace(target,dest) are not offered exactly for those reasons. UStr does not implement DataType: how to turn a UStr in a Str or in an Info is really unclear. How to compare two Unicode strings is also a highly debated topic. UStr does offer .equalRepr(other) and .hashRepr so that a user can make an efficient OrderHash[UStr] while reconsidering their life decisions.

like + but inserts a newline between the two strings

UnitTestLog

Log used internally by the UnitTest library.

The log is written to .out/logs/_base/unit_test_log.log. This log is raw: each call writes exactly the string representation of s, without adding a timestamp and without adding a newline. The UnitTest library is responsible for producing the whole output format.

The live file is intended to be consumed by test tooling while tests are running. The exact format is part of the UnitTest library/runtime contract, not part of this general logging API.

The log is still managed by the same circular-log mechanism as Log: old non-empty logs are moved to stamped archive files, empty logs are deleted, and only a bounded number of archived logs is kept. See also: base.Log

UnitTests

Unit tests This design blends test suites, tests and individual checks. Basically, a test suite is a Test that only calls .test on named Tests, While a Test is a named Test that only calls .check. We can then arbitrary make trees of test suites or by nesting them in other test suites.

A name name is only reported when the name is present. Example code with two test suites. ``` MyTests: UnitTests {:: .test TestCars .test TestPerson } TestCars: Test {:: .let x=... //can declare locals //Test TestCarsCanMove inside test suite TestCars .test TestCarsCanMove: Test {:: .check {..}}

//disabled test with name inside test suite TestCars .disableTest TestCarsCanFly: Test {:: .check {..}}

//unnamed check in the test suite.. possible but not advised .check {Cars#(...).assertEquals(MakeCar#23) }

//A single test can have many checks .test TestCarsCanPark: Test {t-> Block# .if {..} .do{ t.check {..} } .if {..} .do{ t.check {..} } .done} } ``` Example using logs: ``` Events:InMemoryLog[Event]{"Events"} ... .checkWithSys { sys -> Block# .let log=Events.reader(sys); .do { log.clear } .do { actionUnderTest# } .do { log.consume.assertEq({::},Lists#( Event1#(...), Event2#(...), ))} .done } ``` Example checking that an action fails: ``` .checkWithSys { ::.try#{SomethingThatShouldFail#}.assertInfo} ``` Example checking that an action succeeds: ``` .check{SomethingThatShouldSucceed#} ```

_MagicMath

No documentation yet.

Extends: Sealed

Methods

▸.acos(Float):Radian

Returns the arc sine of a value; the returned angle is in [0, pi]. throws if the argument is NaN or its absolute value is greater than 1.

▸.asin(Float):Radian

Returns the arc sine of a value; the returned angle is in [-pi/2, pi/2]. Throws if the argument is NaN or its absolute value is greater than 1, NaN. If the argument is zero, then the result is a zero with the same sign as the argument.

▸.atan(Float):Radian

Returns the arc tangent of a value; the returned angle is in [-pi/2, pi/2]. throws if the argument is NaN. If the argument is zero, then the result is a zero with the same sign as the argument.

▸.atan2(Float,Float):Radian

Returns the angle theta from the conversion of rectangular coordinates (x, y) to polar coordinates (r, theta). This method computes the phase theta by computing an arc tangent of y / x in [-pi to pi] Throws if either x or y is NaN.

▸.hypot(Float,Float):Float

this.hypot(x, y) returns (x** +2.0 + y** +2.0).sqrt. Throws if either argument is NaN

▸.ln(Float):Float

The natural log of the given float, returns: throws if x NaN or < 0, returns negative infinity if x = 0, returns positive infinity if x is positive infinity

▸.log(Float):Float

The log base 10 of the given float, returns: throws if x NaN or < 0, -ve infinity if x = 0, +ve infinity if x is positive infinity, log base 10 of x otherwise;

Several match .getPred

  • Byte.getPred() — `this.getPred` returns ``this - 1``. Throws if `this` is ``0`` (underflow).
  • Int.getPred() — `this.getPred` returns ``this - +1``. Throws if `this` is `Math.minInt` (underflow).
  • Nat.getPred() — `this.getPred` returns ``this - 1``. Throws if `this` is ``0`` (underflow).
  • Float.getPred() — `this.getPred` returns the closest Floating point number smaller than `this`.

Several match .getSucc

  • Byte.getSucc() — `this.getSucc` returns ``this + 1``. Throws if `this` is ``255`` (overflow).
  • Int.getSucc() — `this.getSucc` returns ``this + +1``. Throws if `this` is `Math.maxInt` (overflow).
  • Nat.getSucc() — `this.getSucc` returns ``this + 1``. Throws if `this` is `Math.maxNat` (overflow).
  • Float.getSucc() — `this.getSucc` returns the closest Floating point number larger than `this`.

Several match .getDiv

  • Byte.getDiv(_) — ``this.getDiv(d)`` returns `this` exactly divided by `d`. Throws iff ``d == 0`` or ``this.rem == 1``.
  • Int.getDiv(_) — ``this.getDiv(d)`` returns `this` exactly divided by `d`. Throws iff ``d == 0`` or ``this.rem == 1``.
  • Nat.getDiv(_) — ``this.getDiv(d)`` returns `this` exactly divided by `d`. Throws iff ``d == 0`` or ``rem != 0``.

Several match .abs

  • Int.abs() — `this.abs` returns `this` if ``this >= 0``, ``-this`` otherwise, as a `Nat`.
  • Float.abs() — `this.abs` returns `.some` of `this` if ``this >= 0``, `.some` of ``-this`` if ``this < 0``,
  • Num.abs() — `this.abs` returns the exact absolute value of `this`: `this` if ``this >= 0``, ``-this`` otherwise.
